member.name: T:KeshavSingh.Security.DataProtector
member.summary:
Authenticated symmetric encryption for secrets held at rest (e.g. TOTP shared secrets), using AES-256-GCM. The 256-bit key comes from configuration/Key Vault and is never persisted with the data.
Output layout (Base64): version | keyId | nonce | tag | ciphertext. The two leading bytes are what makes key rotation possible: a value encrypted under an older key still says which key it needs, so can decrypt it while every new write uses the current key. Without them a rotated Encryption:DataKey would silently orphan every stored secret.
Values written before versioning existed have no header. They are recognised by length/shape and decrypted with the current key, so an existing database keeps working with no migration step — re-saving any such secret rewrites it in the new format.

member.name: T:KeshavSingh.Security.PasswordHasher
member.summary: Password hashing using PBKDF2 (Rfc2898) with HMAC-SHA256. No deprecated algorithms. Verification is constant-time. Hash format: "iterations.salt.hash" (both segments Base64), which is self-describing so the cost can be raised later.

member.summary: A hash of a fixed dummy password, for verifying against when no account matched. Doing the same PBKDF2 work on the "unknown user" path is what stops response timing from revealing which email addresses have accounts. Built once — it is not a secret.

member.name: T:KeshavSingh.Security.TokenHasher
member.summary: SHA-256 hashing for high-entropy secrets (refresh tokens, backup codes, email OTPs) so only hashes are stored. SHA-256 is appropriate here because these values are random and high-entropy — unlike passwords, they do not need a slow KDF. Also generates cryptographically random opaque tokens and numeric OTPs.

member.name: T:KeshavSingh.Security.TotpService
member.summary:
RFC 6238 time-based one-time passwords for authenticator apps (Google / Microsoft Authenticator, etc.).
NOTE ON HMAC-SHA1: TOTP is specified over HMAC-SHA1 and authenticator apps default to it — using SHA-256 here would make codes mismatch on most apps. This is HMAC (a keyed MAC), not SHA-1 used as a digest or signature: the SHA-1 collision weaknesses do not apply to HMAC-SHA1, which remains sound. This is a deliberate, documented exception to the "no SHA-1" guideline for interop only.

member.name: M:KeshavSingh.Security.TotpService.VerifyCode(System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Verifies a user-supplied code against the secret, tolerating clock drift.
member.remarks: Prefer : on its own this cannot reject a replay, because a TOTP code stays valid for the whole drift window and nothing here remembers that one was spent. RFC 6238 §5.2 requires the verifier to accept a given code only once.

member.name: M:KeshavSingh.Security.TotpService.TryVerifyCode(System.String,System.String,System.Nullable{System.Int64},System.Int64@)
member.summary: Verifies a code and reports which time step matched, so the caller can persist it and pass it back as next time. Any code whose step is at or before the last one already spent is refused — that is what makes a captured code single-use instead of valid for the rest of its ~90-second window.
member.param: The step of this user's last accepted code, or null if none.
The step that matched; persist it on success.
